newsitem.title: CHINA: Chinese trek to Beijing to mark HK recovery.
newsitem.headline: Chinese trek to Beijing to mark HK recovery.

text.p: The final countdown to the recovery of Hong Kong has been a powerful magnet, attracting people from around China to the nation's capital to usher in the start of a new and post-colonial era.

From remote corners of the country they made their pilgrimage, enduring long hours of bumpy bus rides or hard-seat overnight trains to catch a glimpse of the gala celebration in Beijing marking the end of 156 years of British rule over Hong Kong.

Many were visibly disappointed when unarmed police and paramilitary forces cleared the throngs of visitors from the capital's central Tiananmen Square on Monday afternoon to prepare for official celebrations this evening.
"I'm disappointed," said one man as he left the square with his friends ahead of the advancing ranks of police and street sweepers.
"We came all the way from Nanjing to see this," he said.

Nanjing, an eastern city now just few hours by train from Shanghai, was where China and Britain agreed in 1842 on the terms that ended the Opium War, including the cession of Hong Kong as a British colony.

China has loudly proclaimed the recovery of the territory as marking an end to its national humiliation at the hands of Western imperial powers. State media have fed the public with a steady diet of news and propaganda on the British colony's return at the stroke of midnight on Monday.
Hong Kong is out of reach for most Chinese, and Beijing is the next best place to be.
Some 100,000 people have been invited to the official party in Beijing to watch a huge digital clock count down the final minutes of British rule over Hong Kong.
They will be treated to a pageant of song and dance before a barrage of fireworks lights up the midnight sky as the territory formally becomes Chinese territory.
Huang Fucheng, a farmer from Heilongjiang on the Russian border, is not on the guest list but he spent more than 30 hours on trains in his journey to witness the festivities.
"I'm thrilled to be part of this," he said, shortly before police told him to leave Tiananmen Square. "I'm not tired at all."
Li Yuqing, who normally spends his time keeping an eye on his stock portfolio, said he took a 14-hour train from central Wuhan to Beijing to share in the thrill of the historic moment.
"This is history. I didn't want to miss it."
Fortunately for Li, China's stock markets are closed on Monday and Tuesday to commemorate the colony's return.
"One day I would like to be able to trade on the Hong Kong market," he said.
Wang Jieping brought his wife and two-year-old daughter on a 10-hour train ride from Inner Mongolia to join in the fun.
As police motioned the crowd to leave Tiananmen Square, Wang's tearful daughter had clearly had enough of the afternoon heat. But for Wang, the day was far from over.
"I will stay as close to the square as I can," he said.
